gloss_terse: Omri — personal name borne by four Israelites, most notably the sixth king of the northern kingdom
gloss_readable: A Hebrew proper name meaning possibly 'my sheaf' or 'pupil of Yah.' Most prominently, Omri was the powerful king of Israel who founded Samaria as his new capital (1 Kgs 16:16–28). So lasting was his dynasty's reputation that Assyrian records continued to call Israel 'the house of Omri' (Bit-Humri) long after his line had ended. The Moabite Stone likewise names him. Three other men bear this name: a Benjaminite (1 Chr 7:8), a Judahite (9:4), and a chief of Issachar under David (27:18).

senses.1: The proper name Omri, applied to four distinct individuals. The most prominent is King Omri of Israel, army commander acclaimed king by the troops at Gibbethon, who reigned from Tirzah and then built Samaria (1 Kgs 16:16–28). Assyrian cuneiform (Humri) and the Mesha Stele attest his international significance. Three lesser figures in Chronicles also bear the name.

gloss_terse: Simple, naive, gullible — an inexperienced person open to influence, for good or ill, in Wisdom literature
gloss_readable: Derived from the root patah ('to be open, entice'), this adjective describes a person whose mind is open but undiscerning — easily swayed toward wisdom or folly. In Proverbs, the peti is the primary addressee of instruction: lacking shrewdness (1:4), believing every word (14:15), and loving simplicity rather than knowledge (1:22). Yet the term is not purely negative; Psalm 116:6 declares that the LORD preserves the simple. Multilingual translations capture this range well — Spanish 'sencillo/simple,' French 'simple' — highlighting the tension between innocence and gullibility.

senses.1: A naive or inexperienced person who is open to persuasion, whether toward wisdom or folly. Proverbs presents the peti as the young hearer who must choose between Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly (Prov 9:4, 16). The term sits between the wise (chakham) and the fool (kesil), suggesting a redeemable naivete. Psalm 19:7 affirms that God's testimony makes the simple wise, while Psalm 116:6 shows divine care for the guileless.

gloss_terse: Deep darkness, shadow of death — intense, impenetrable gloom used poetically of mortal peril and divine mystery
gloss_readable: A striking poetic compound (tsalmaveth) traditionally rendered 'shadow of death,' though modern scholarship often reads it as an abstract noun meaning 'deep darkness.' Whether from tsel + maveth or from a root cognate to Arabic and Ethiopic words for blackness, the word evokes the most profound imaginable gloom. Job uses it seven times to describe the underworld and extremes of despair (Job 3:5; 10:21–22). Its most beloved occurrence is Psalm 23:4, where the faithful walk through the valley of tsalmaveth fearing no evil. Amos 5:8 speaks of God turning tsalmaveth into morning light.

senses.1: Intensely deep darkness understood as the deepest conceivable shadow, often paralleled with choshekh ('darkness') and layilah ('night'). Traditionally parsed as 'shadow of death' (tsel + maveth), yielding the unforgettable image of Psalm 23:4. In Job it characterizes Sheol and utter despair (Job 10:21–22; 12:22). Amos 5:8 and Jeremiah 13:16 use it for cosmic or threatened darkness that only God can transform into light.

gloss_terse: Kadesh — a sacred wilderness site in the Negev where Israel encamped during the exodus wanderings
gloss_readable: Meaning 'sacred' or 'holy place,' Kadesh (also called Kadesh-barnea) was a major stopping point in Israel's wilderness journeys, situated in the wilderness of Zin near the border of Edom. It served as the base from which the twelve spies were sent into Canaan (Num 13:26) and where Miriam died and Moses struck the rock at Meribah (Num 20:1–13). The site appears across the Pentateuch, in Judges, Psalms, and Ezekiel's ideal boundary descriptions. German translations sometimes render the meaning directly as 'Heiligkeit' (holiness), reflecting the etymological sense.

senses.1: The place name Kadesh, a wilderness oasis in the Negev marking the southern boundary of Canaan. Israel encamped here during the exodus, and pivotal events occurred at this site: the sending of the spies (Num 13:26), the rebellion at Meribah (Num 20:1–13), and failed negotiations with Edom (Num 20:14–16). Ezekiel uses it to demarcate the ideal future boundary (Ezek 47:19; 48:28). Psalm 29:8 speaks of the wilderness of Kadesh shaking at God's voice.

gloss_terse: Lamentation, dirge, funeral song — a mournful poem composed to bewail the dead or a catastrophe
gloss_readable: This feminine noun denotes a formal poetic lament, typically composed in the distinctive qinah meter (3+2 stress pattern) that became the hallmark of biblical dirge poetry. David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 1:17) is introduced with this word. Ezekiel receives special command to 'raise a qinah' over Tyre (27:2), Egypt (32:2), and Israel's princes (19:1). Jeremiah calls women to learn and teach the dirge (Jer 9:19). The term appears alongside words for mourning (evel) and wailing (nehi), situating it firmly within Israel's rich tradition of ritual grief.

senses.1: A formal dirge or funeral song, characterized by the qinah rhythm of uneven half-lines (3+2 beats). Used for laments over the dead (2 Sam 1:17, David over Saul) and prophetic funeral songs over nations and cities. Ezekiel is repeatedly commanded to 'lift up a qinah' (Ezek 19:1; 26:17; 27:2; 28:12; 32:2). Jeremiah pairs it with weeping (Jer 9:10) and calls mourning women to teach it (9:19). Spanish 'lamentación/lamento' and French 'lamentation' preserve the formal tone.

gloss_terse: Keilah — a fortified city in the Shephelah of Judah, famous as the site David rescued from the Philistines
gloss_readable: Keilah was a walled city in the lowlands of Judah, about eight miles northwest of Hebron. Its most dramatic biblical episode is David's rescue of the city from a Philistine grain raid (1 Sam 23:1–13), after which God warned David that Keilah's citizens would betray him to Saul, prompting his departure. The city appears in Joshua's tribal allotment for Judah (Josh 15:44) and again in Nehemiah among those who repaired sections of Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:17–18). It may correspond to the Tell el-Amarna city Qiltu.

senses.1: The toponym Keilah, a fortified town in the Shephelah of Judah near the Philistine frontier. David liberated it from Philistine attack but fled when God revealed the inhabitants would surrender him to Saul (1 Sam 23:1–13). Listed among Judah's towns in Joshua 15:44 and among post-exilic districts contributing to Nehemiah's wall rebuilding (Neh 3:17–18). Possibly identified with modern Khirbet Qila and the Amarna-era Qiltu.

gloss_terse: Reubenite — a member or descendant of the tribe of Reuben, Israel's firstborn son
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective identifies persons belonging to the tribe of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. The Reubenites received their territorial allotment east of the Jordan in the Transjordan tableland (Deut 3:12, 16; Josh 13:8). They appear regularly alongside the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh as the three Transjordanian tribes who crossed the Jordan armed to help conquer Canaan (Josh 1:12; 22:1). Reubenite territory later fell to Moabite and Assyrian encroachment (2 Kgs 10:33; 1 Chr 5:26). The term occurs with the article as a collective noun or without it for individuals (1 Chr 11:42).

senses.1: A gentilic designating members of the tribe of Reuben, used both of individuals (1 Chr 11:42) and collectively with the article for the entire clan. The Reubenites settled east of the Jordan (Deut 3:12; Josh 13:8), frequently mentioned together with the Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh. Their territory was exposed to foreign incursion: Hazael's raids (2 Kgs 10:33) and eventual Assyrian exile under Tiglath-pileser (1 Chr 5:26).

gloss_terse: Supplications, earnest pleas for mercy — heartfelt entreaties directed to God or a superior for grace
gloss_readable: This plural abstract noun (tachanunim) expresses urgent, earnest pleas for undeserved favor. It derives from the root chanan ('to be gracious') and occurs only in the plural, underscoring the intensity and repetition of such appeals. Nearly always directed to God, it frequently parallels tefillah ('prayer') as in Psalm 143:1 and Daniel 9:3, 17. The Psalms speak of the 'voice of my supplications' (Ps 28:2, 6; 31:22; 86:6; 130:2), while Jeremiah pairs it with weeping (Jer 3:21; 31:9). Proverbs 18:23 offers its sole human-to-human use: the poor speak tachanunim.

senses.1: Earnest, repeated entreaties for mercy and grace, overwhelmingly addressed to God. The plural-only form intensifies the urgency of the appeal. Paired with tefillah in formal prayer contexts (Ps 143:1; Dan 9:3, 17) and with weeping in prophetic grief (Jer 3:21; 31:9). The Psalms especially treasure the phrase qol tachanunim, 'the voice of my supplications' (Ps 28:2, 6; 86:6; 130:2). Proverbs 18:23 uniquely applies it to a poor person pleading before the rich.

gloss_terse: Tirzah — a proper name meaning 'pleasure, beauty,' borne by a daughter of Zelophehad and an early Israelite capital
gloss_readable: Tirzah (meaning 'delight' or 'beauty') serves as both a personal and a geographic name. As a person, she is one of the five daughters of Zelophehad who successfully petitioned Moses for inheritance rights (Num 27:1; 36:11). As a place, Tirzah was an old Canaanite royal city (Josh 12:24) that became the first capital of the northern kingdom before Omri moved the seat to Samaria (1 Kgs 15:21–16:23). Song of Solomon 6:4 celebrates a beloved as 'beautiful as Tirzah,' placing the city alongside Jerusalem as a byword for loveliness.

senses.1: The proper noun Tirzah used for both a woman and a city. As a personal name, one of Zelophehad's five daughters whose inheritance claim established a legal precedent for female land rights (Num 26:33; 27:1; 36:11; Josh 17:3). As a place name, an ancient Canaanite city (Josh 12:24) that served as the northern kingdom's capital from Jeroboam through the early years of Omri's reign (1 Kgs 14:17–16:23). Song of Solomon 6:4 invokes its beauty alongside Jerusalem.

gloss_terse: The ninth — ordinal number marking the ninth position in a sequence of time, persons, or objects
gloss_readable: The ordinal form of tesha ('nine'), used to mark the ninth item in various ordered sequences throughout the Hebrew Bible. It designates the ninth month of the year (2 Kgs 25:1; Jer 36:9, 22), the ninth day of a month, the ninth tribal offering in Numbers 7:60, and the ninth position in genealogical or military rosters (1 Chr 12:12; 24:11; 25:16; 27:12). The form appears with the article (hatteshi'i) for both masculine and feminine referents, reflecting standard Hebrew ordinal usage.

senses.1: The ordinal 'ninth,' marking position in calendrical, ceremonial, and administrative sequences. Applied to the ninth month (the month of Kislev, 2 Kgs 25:1; Jer 36:9), the ninth day, the ninth tribal leader's offering (Num 7:60), and the ninth division of priestly or military courses (1 Chr 12:12; 24:11; 25:16; 27:12). Spanish 'noveno,' English 'ninth,' and French forms consistently reflect a straightforward ordinal sense.
